newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Conference looks at E. Europe prostitute trade.
newsitem.headline: Conference looks at E. Europe prostitute trade.

text.p: Prostitutes plying a lucrative cross-border sex trade in economically-depressed eastern Europe should be treated as migrant workers, speakers at a conference in Hungary said on Friday.
"Prostitutes are...migrant workers in a way," said Nicoleta Druta, an official dealing with gender issues for the Romanian office of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Bucharest.
"Not all prostitutes are forced into prostitution by pimps. They are forced by their economic situation...they are forced to work abroad as prostitutes....

"We cannot call them prostitutes any longer. We have to call them sex workers to change the way they are treated by the civil authorities," she told a conference on trafficking in women sponsored by the International Organisation for Migration (IOM).
Frank Laczko, Budapest representative of the Switzerland-based IOM, said the sex industry had changed in Hungary and western Europe.
"It is increasingly dominated by migrant prostitutes who have absolutely no rights to even be living in those countries, let alone be prostitutes," he said.
"The thrust of policy is mainly to protect the community against the prostitution industry," Laczko said on the opening day of the two-day conference.
"It offers relatively little protection for the local prostitutes and the issue of protection for migrant prostitutes is completely ignored."

Lieutenant Colonel Akos Borai of the Hungarian national police said a third of prostitutes working in clubs, massage parlours and other indoor venues in Budapest are foreigners, mainly from countries to the east of Hungary.
"There could be 15,000 (foreigners) or there could be many more," he said.

"This also involves huge amounts of money and that's why there are such bloody fights," he said, adding that there had been killings involving members of the Ukrainian mafia which he said controlled the Budapest sex club scene.
"Somebody said it amounts to hundreds of billions of forints (millions of dollars) but I don't know where the figure would come from since the money is laundered so well," he said.
He added that he thought Budapest had been unfairly portrayed in some press reports as "the Bangkok of eastern Europe" for child sex activities.
He said he knew of only "two or three such cases and they were not such big cases.

Lenke Feher, a lawyer from the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, said the collapse of communism in eastern Europe in the late 1980s ended the system of full employment that kept many people afloat, and forced women to turn to prostitution.
"As we were not accustomed to unemployment, this created more tension than in some other countries," she said.

"Prostitution is going on in an organised form," she said. "It has become globalised and industrialised using new technologies. Even Hungary, which was a country of origin (for prostitutes), is now a transit point and country of destination."
